content: The transition from pediatric to adult healthcare services often results in a decline in health outcomes for adolescents with chronic conditions. Transitional care aims to address this gap by facilitating a structured and planned movement of adolescents and young adults with chronic medical conditions from child-centered to adult-oriented healthcare systems. To design effective services for this population, it is essential to identify interventions that work and understand the barriers and facilitators to their success. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions designed to improve the transition of care for adolescents moving from pediatric to adult health services. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), controlled before-and-after studies (CBAs), and interrupted time-series studies (ITSs). Adolescents with chronic conditions requiring ongoing care, their families, and healthcare providers were the focus of these studies. Data were extracted independently by two reviewers, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Four RCTs involving 238 participants were included in the review. These studies evaluated various interventions, including: 1. A two-day workshop-based transition preparation program for adolescents with spina bifida. 2. A nurse-led, one-on-one teaching session supplemented by a health passport for adolescents with congenital heart disease. 3. A weband SMS-based educational intervention for adolescents with various chronic conditions. 4. A structured, comprehensive transition program with a transition coordinator for adolescents with type 1 diabetes. The findings were as follows: A nurse-led, one-on-one intervention and a technology-based intervention showed slight improvements in transitional readiness and chronic disease self-management at sixto eight-month follow-ups. However, the evidence was of low certainty. For example, self-management scores measured using the TRAQ tool showed modest improvements (MD 0.20; 95% CI -0.16 to 0.56 and MD 0.43; 95% CI -0.09 to 0.95). Self-advocacy scores also showed small gains (MD 0.37; 95% CI -0.06 to 0.80). The two-day workshop for adolescents with spina bifida showed little to no improvement in self-care practices or general health behaviors, as measured by the DSCPI-90© tool. Two studies assessed the use of health services. A technology-based intervention and a comprehensive transition program showed a slight increase in the likelihood of adolescents initiating contact with healthcare professionals. However, the evidence was of low certainty (RR 4.87; 95% CI 0.24 to 98.12 and RR 1.50; 95% CI 0.32 to 6.94, respectively). A nurse-led, one-on-one intervention for adolescents with congenital heart disease slightly improved disease knowledge (MD 14; 95% CI 2.67 to 25.33). However, disease-specific outcomes in two studies showed little to no difference between intervention and control groups. In adolescents with type 1 diabetes, follow-up HbA1c levels increased by 1.2% for each percentage increase in baseline HbA1c, regardless of the treatment group (1.2%; 95% CI 0.4 to 1.9; P = 0.01). Interventions showed little to no impact on well-being or quality of life, as measured by the PARS III or PedsQ tools. For example, the technology-based intervention and the two-day workshop for spina bifida patients showed no significant differences between groups (MD 1.29; 95% CI -4.49 to 7.07). A study involving four telephone support calls from a transition coordinator showed little to no difference in the rates of transfer from pediatric to adult diabetes services (RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.08). However, there was a slight reduction in the risk of disease-related hospital admissions at 12-month follow-up (RR 0.29; 95% CI 0.03 to 2.40). The authors concluded that the available evidence, derived from four small studies with a total of 238 participants, is limited in scope and certainty. The interventions evaluated addressed a narrow range of clinical conditions, and follow-up periods of four to 12 months may not have been sufficient to observe meaningful changes, as the transition process is lengthy. While some studies showed improvements in disease knowledge, self-efficacy, and confidence, the overall certainty of the evidence was low, preventing firm conclusions about the effectiveness of these interventions. Further research with rigorous evaluation, longer follow-up periods, and a focus on clinical outcomes is needed to better understand the impact of transitional care models.
